song.title: Because It’s Springtime!
song.author: Mark, Helen and Naomi Johnson
song.summary: A simple song with plenty of repetition and bounce, which make this perfect for younger voices. Explore and enjoy the signs of spring and celebrate ‘every little thing’ that ‘has started coming to life!’
song.teachingTips:
• This is a bouncy, happy song, so try to reflect this in your singing style, particularly in the verses. 
  • Contrast this with a smoother, more lyrical style on ‘spring has sprung’, ‘blooming bright’ and ‘‘new’ has come’ in the choruses.
  • Watch out for the syncopated rhythm on ‘they’re’ and ‘me’ in verse 1 (and in the corresponding places in verses 2 and 3).
  • Notice there’s no ‘And’ on the penultimate line of verse 3, which is different to earlier in the verse – so it’s just ‘Everywhere ’round us there’s life to be found’.

assembly.title: Light and Colour
assembly.description: This assembly encourages us to open our eyes to the colours of springtime, talking about our favourite colours, noticing the extra daylight and appreciating nature's use of colour and light.

assembly.title: Extra Energy
assembly.description: What wakes you up in the morning? From birdsong to sprouting leaves and Easter eggs, this assembly helps us to celebrate all the energy of springtime.

assembly.title: Turning Over a New Leaf
assembly.description: This assembly looks at new leaves and growth in nature and helps us all to look within ourselves to see where we might want to ‘turn over a new leaf’ too.

assembly.title: Metamorphosis
assembly.description: Looking at change and understanding that there are things to be enjoyed at every stage of life.

assembly.title: Feeling Awake
assembly.description: This assembly uses The Parable of the Sower to reflect on what is needed to be ‘awake and ready for action’ in school.

resources.title: The Arrival Of Spring
resources.content:
[{"key":"e6936f3f06a10794","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

David Hockney (b. 1937) recently made a series of works responding to the changing colours of woodland (Wold Woods, Yorkshire) throughout the four seasons. He created oil paintings, charcoal drawings and iPad drawings, and recorded films as part of this series of work. 

How could the children use the influence of Hockney's work to respond to the colours and changing nature of spring? 

  • Take photos of the school grounds (field/flower beds/nature area) thoughout the seasons to see how things have grown and changed. (Record in a school/class calendar to carry on throughout the year.)
  • Record films of the school grounds. 
  • Incorporate technology to embrace Hockney's style: use iPads or tablets to create spring drawings and play back the creation of these to watch how they form the finished work. 
","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}}]

resources.title: Acrostic Spring Poem
resources.content:
[{"key":"482384050edd82de","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Compose an Acrostic Spring Poem. As a class, brainstorm and collect ideas for each of the letters of SPRING. Then, ask the children to write some SPRING poems developing their favourite ideas/words into a line for each letter. 

  • Sunshine peeping through the grey,
  • Petals sprouting, on their way.
  • Rainbows arching overhead, 
  • Insects waking from their beds,
  • New life blooming everywhere,
  • Growing wild, without a care!
","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}}]

resources.title: Spring celebrations
resources.content:
[{"key":"1b2cc4940756aede","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

The arrival of spring is an important time of year, with celebrations taking place to mark the occasion all around the world. What spring traditions and celebrations<\/strong> do the children already know about? Find out about how Easter is celebrated in different countries. Other spring festivals include the Songkran Water Festival in Thailand, the Hanami cherry blossom festival in Japan, and the colourful Holi festival in India. Locate these places on a globe or atlas and ask groups to research a particular celebration and present their findings to the class.<\/p>\n","title":"","noMargin":false}}]

resources.title: Syncopated Percussion
resources.content:
[{"key":"93e17ad73b02d0f1","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To explore tresillo rhythm
  • To clap along in time with the song
  • To perform a percussion accompaniment
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"5a9535c7181d9cfe","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

A good sense of pulse; untuned percussion, e.g. claves, guiros, shakers

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"4a1118cfa6b9d8f9","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Listen carefully to the backing track. See if the children can clap along with the following syncopated rhythm, which emphasizes quaver beats 1, 4 and 7 of the bar:

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"5925456c50b9697e","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicActivities/syncopatedpercussion-16727503575hsdx.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"d4c66f09cdd604e0","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

This is also known as a 3 + 3 + 2 or ‘tresillo’ rhythm, which is the rhythm that gets your toes tapping and hips swaying in Latin American music. See if the children can gently move from one foot to the other on beats 1 and 3 of the bar (or beats 1 and 5 if you are counting in quavers) as they clap along with the track. 

Now transfer this rhythm to various untuned percussion instruments such as claves, guiros and shakers to create a rhythmic accompaniment to the verses of the song.

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"96b2371cb3559164","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Listen to the bass line played by the left hand of the pianist in New Orleans Blues by Jelly Roll Morton, whcih features the tresillo rhythm.

","title":"Listen","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/listen-01-1615991956LRT6z.png"}},{"key":"6908833b114df451","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k24fD36Zurk","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"bb2ad9e6130e5ba1","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

For more about the origin of the ‘tresillo’ rhythm and some more contemporary examples, watch the following clip. It’s a bit long to play in its entirety, but you might want to play some short clips to the children.

","title":"Look","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/icons-look-280x280-16159933936d8D7.png"}},{"key":"352781b2e2b1a8bd","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DZ_yT_ukkKA&t=53s","title":"","noMargin":false}}]
resources.summary: Explore the tresillo rhythm by clapping along with and moving to the backing track. Listen to some examples in other pieces of music and then transfer this rhythm to untuned percussion instruments to create a rhythmic accompaniment to the verses.
